content: Innovative strategies that actively involve patients and their family caregivers should be developed or further explored to enhance the detection of infection signs and promote timely symptom reporting. For example, surgical site infections (SSIs) frequently occur after hospital discharge, and patient-reported data can significantly enhance surveillance efforts. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on the core components of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs emphasize the importance of healthcare-associated infection (HAI) surveillance at both national and acute healthcare facility levels. Specifically, the guidelines recommend the establishment of national HAI surveillance programs and networks that include mechanisms for timely data feedback and benchmarking. These programs aim to reduce HAIs and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Although the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low quality, the recommendation is considered strong due to the critical role of surveillance in guiding effective IPC interventions. Evidence from one study indicates that timely feedback mechanisms within HAI surveillance programs, particularly in sub-national networks, can lead to significant reductions in HAI rates. While the evidence did not meet the stringent Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) criteria, additional studies reviewed by the guideline development group (GDG) demonstrated the benefits of national surveillance and feedback in reducing HAIs. Despite the limited evidence, the GDG strongly supports the establishment of national HAI surveillance programs with timely feedback mechanisms for benchmarking purposes. However, the implementation of such programs is resource-intensive, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), requiring financial and human resources, laboratory support, and expertise. The GDG also highlighted the importance of national HAI surveillance systems in strengthening public health capacity and essential public health functions. These systems are crucial for the early detection of outbreaks, including those characterized by specific pathogens or AMR patterns. National microbiological data on HAI etiology and resistance patterns provide valuable information for antimicrobial use policies and AMR-related strategies. The GDG emphasized that HAI surveillance data are essential for developing and implementing effective IPC interventions. Establishing a national HAI surveillance program requires full support and engagement from governments and relevant authorities, including the allocation of appropriate budgets and resources to ensure effective coordination and data sharing at the country level. National surveillance systems should have clear objectives, standardized case definitions, methods for detecting infections, and processes for data analysis and reporting. International guidelines on HAI definitions are important, but their adaptation at the country level is critical for successful implementation. The GDG also recommended the development of national guidelines referencing international standards, including standardized definitions and techniques for conducting surveillance. If national guidelines are unavailable, they should be developed, complemented by a national training program to ensure consistent application of surveillance guidelines and tools. Clear reporting lines for HAI surveillance data from healthcare facilities to the national level should be established. National HAI surveillance systems should also be integrated into public health infection surveillance systems, particularly linking to national AMR surveillance systems, as healthcare facilities are high-risk settings for AMR selection and spread. The GDG underscored the critical role of microbiology and laboratory capacity in national and hospital-based HAI and AMR surveillance. Standardized definitions and laboratory methods should be adopted to ensure data quality. Proper sample collection and transport procedures are essential, and national IPC programs should develop standardized protocols for facility-level implementation. Microbiological data analysis should provide information on the etiology and AMR patterns of the most frequent and severe infections. High-quality microbiological support from at least one national reference laboratory is crucial for an effective national IPC surveillance program. National HAI surveillance data are vital for policymakers to prioritize and develop evidence-based IPC standards and influence decisions on appropriate AMR strategies and policies. IPC activities should respond to actual needs, and national surveillance systems for HAI and AMR patterns are essential components for assessing the impact of IPC interventions. These systems also contribute to public health capacity building and the early detection of outbreaks and new AMR patterns. The GDG reviewed evidence on the impact of national surveillance on HAIs, including studies showing significant reductions in HAI rates when national surveillance programs with timely feedback mechanisms are implemented. For example, studies in Germany, France, Italy, Finland, Switzerland, and the USA demonstrated reductions in SSIs, MRSA, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and other HAIs. Longer-duration surveillance programs were associated with greater reductions in infection rates. Despite the lack of studies on patient values and preferences regarding national HAI surveillance, the GDG is confident that patients, healthcare providers, and policymakers would value such programs, particularly in the context of AMR and international public health priorities. While resource-intensive, the GDG believes the benefits of national HAI surveillance programs outweigh the costs, especially when considering their role in guiding IPC strategies and interventions. Education and training will likely be required to standardize surveillance processes nationwide. In conclusion, despite the limited quality of evidence, the GDG strongly supports national HAI surveillance as a critical component of IPC programs, particularly in addressing AMR and strengthening public health systems.
